title: MIT Researchers Publish Electrochemically Mediated CO₂ Capture — Flexible, Renewable-Compatible Carbon Removal
detail: A team at MIT published research on June 4, 2026, on electrochemically mediated CO2 capture (EMCC) — a new approach to carbon removal that uses electricity rather than heat to drive CO2 separation from industrial exhaust streams and ambient air. Supported by the MIT Climate and Sustainability Consortium (MCSC), the research demonstrates that EMCC can be powered by variable renewable electricity, making capture intensity adjustable in real time to match renewable supply — a critical advantage over conventional thermal CCS, which requires continuous operation. The electrochemical approach shows potential to reduce both the energy intensity and cost of carbon capture in hard-to-abate sectors including cement, steel, and chemical manufacturing. The MIT team emphasized that while significant engineering challenges remain before commercial deployment, the technology pathway offers a more flexible complement to thermal CCS, particularly in regions with high renewable penetration. The research was published as part of the MCSC's broader roadmap to accelerate scalable climate solutions through industry-academic partnerships.

title: Australia Utility Solar+Wind Generation Up 10% Year-on-Year in May 2026 — Victoria Sets Wind Record
detail: Rystad Energy data published in early June 2026 showed Australian utility-scale solar and wind combined generated 4.6 TWh in May 2026, a 10% year-on-year increase from 4.2 TWh in May 2025. Victoria set a new monthly wind generation record, producing 1,079 GWh of wind power in May — the state's highest monthly wind output on record. The streak of annual output increases reflects consistent capacity additions across the National Electricity Market (NEM). April 2026 had already posted a 24% year-on-year gain at 4.7 TWh. Australia's renewable buildout is accelerating under the federal government's 82% renewable electricity by 2030 target, with large-scale solar and wind additions continuing to outpace coal retirements.
